turns.prompt: Hash table lookups are usually described as O(1). When can a lookup become O(n), and what does the table do to keep operations fast as more and more keys are added?
turns.answer: A hash table gives O(1) look‑ups only on average, assuming the hash function distributes keys uniformly across the buckets. If many keys end up in the same bucket—because the hash function is poor or an attacker forces collisions—the bucket becomes a list (or probe chain) that must be scanned linearly, so a single lookup can degrade to O(n) in the worst case. To avoid that, implementations track the load factor (the ratio of stored entries to bucket count) and, when it exceeds a threshold, allocate a larger array and re‑hash all existing keys into it. The resize operation costs O(n) but happens infrequently, so inserts and look‑ups remain amortised O(1) under normal conditions.
